summary:
Vanuatu has never criminalised same-sex conduct, and the sources record no documented pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors. The operative risk for a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming traveller comes from official posture rather than from statute: in November 2024 the Ministry of Justice and Community Services was directed to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion. National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 had targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, with V-Pride framed as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values. That framing invites suspicion of advocacy or promotion rather than of private conduct, and a foreign visitor who is visibly gender-nonconforming has no standing as a resident to argue the distinction.

Parliament amended the Marriage Act in November 2024 to define marriage as the union of a male and a female. Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed that same-sex marriages cannot be registered and that pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law. The amendment removes any assumption that a partnered trans visitor's relationship would be recognised locally.

Country coverage describes Vanuatu as socially conservative, advises gay and lesbian travellers and citizens to avoid public displays of affection, and reports no active gay scene. There is no general legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and no general prohibition of employment discrimination on that basis. Two narrow provisions exist: Section 18.2(f) of the Teaching Service Act 2013 bars the Vanuatu Teaching Service Commission from discriminating on the ground of "sexual preference" in recruitment, promotion, professional development, transfer and staff management, and Section 2(2)(j) of the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024 bars digital communications that denigrate a person by reason of, among other grounds, sexual orientation.

Prosecutorial practice runs against that hostility. The Office of the Public Prosecutor's Prosecution Policy 2003, the Prosecutors Code (Gazette no. 13 of 2017) and its General Principles on vulnerable witnesses in sexual and gender-based violence cases require prosecutors to disregard sexual preference and to treat discrimination or hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity as factors weighing toward prosecution. Vanuatu signed the United Nations joint statement on ending violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2011.
tangentialFactors:
Same-sex partners receive no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes instead, a gap identified at the first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop held by the VPride Foundation and the Vanuatu Women's Centre in October 2016. USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted case of violence against lesbians and a near-invisible LGBTI presence in the courts, which indicates that remedies exist on paper but are rarely used.

Organised LGBTI advocacy has drawn opposition from churches, officials and chiefs since the VPride Foundation's founding, and the 2024 policy initiative extends that pressure into formal rule-making. Against this, the foundation marked the International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia in Vanuatu for the first time in 2016 and continues to advocate LGBTQ rights and freedom of speech, holding awareness events.
localsOnly:
Residents have no general statutory protection against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing or services. The Teaching Service Act 2013 exemption covers only the teaching service, and the Harmful Digital Communications Act 2024 protects against denigrating digital communications referencing sexual orientation but does not operate as a general equality law.

Same-sex couples cannot register a marriage, and pastors are barred by the November 2024 amendment from performing ceremonies contrary to the redefined Marriage Act. Same-sex partners also fall outside the Family Protection Act 2008, so domestic-violence recourse runs through the penal code.

Prosecutors are directed by the 2003 Prosecution Policy, the Prosecutors Code gazetted in 2017 and the General Principles on vulnerable witnesses to disregard sexual preference and to weigh hostility based on sexual orientation or gender identity in favour of bringing a charge. The VPride Foundation, established as a Ni-Vanuatu advocacy organisation, remains the principal domestic body pressing LGBTQ rights and freedom of speech.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources disagree on the VPride Foundation's founding year: Sista's 2016 report gives 2014, while the country coverage gives 2009. The discrepancy is unresolved and does not affect the risk assessment.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, the amendment of sex markers on passports or identity documents, or whether entry and immigration screening could disclose a visitor's gender history. Care access, including hormone supply and trans-specific medical services, is likewise not sourced here.

The November 2024 committee was tasked with drafting a national policy; whether that policy has since been issued, and how any resulting rule would be enforced against visitors rather than residents, is not documented in the available material. There is also no sourced data on trans-specific violence, so the absence of a documented pattern reflects an absence of reporting rather than a positive finding of safety.
